slides.title: Ocean: A Vast Storehouse
slides.kicker: The sea holds food, fuel and minerals
bullets: Oceans are vast storehouses; materials and features of the ocean with intrinsic or economic value are called marine resources.
Marine resources fall into two broad categories: Marine Living Resources and Marine Non-living Resources.
They range from fish, seafood and coral reefs to oil, natural gas, minerals, sand and gravel, and tidal and wave energy.
slides.note: Grade 8 me natural resources padha tha? Ab ocean wala chapter!

slides.title: Living Resources of the Sea
slides.kicker: From shelf fish to deep ocean fish
bullets: Coastal or neritic fish live within the continental shelf at depths of 0 to 200 metres.
Oceanic fish live beyond the continental shelf, at depths greater than 200 metres.
Fish groups include epipelagic, pelagic, demersal, benthopelagic and benthic fish.
The sea also gives bioactive natural products from marine bioorganisms and submerged aquatic vegetation.
slides.note: 200 m is the magic line between shelf and open ocean.

slides.title: Minerals and Ocean Energy
slides.kicker: Oil today, tides and wind tomorrow
bullets: Non-living resources include minerals, sand and gravel, and deep-sea minerals.
Conventional energy sources include oil, natural gas and gas hydrates.
Non-conventional energy includes biofuels, offshore wind and ocean energy.
Ocean mechanical energy covers tidal, wave and current energy, while OTEC uses ocean thermal energy conversion.
slides.note: Blue energy means renewable power from the sea.

slides.title: Why Marine Resources Matter
bullets: Marine resources are vital for food security, economic activities and maintaining a healthy environment.
Fish are a major source of protein, while fishing and aquaculture support important industries and livelihoods.
About 90 per cent of global trade by volume is carried by sea, and coastal tourism is a multi-billion dollar industry.
Countries with long coastlines, like India, gain fishing, trade and tourism livelihoods for millions of people.

slides.title: Use Resources Responsibly
slides.kicker: Take from the sea, but wisely
bullets: Marine resources must be used responsibly without disturbing marine ecosystems.
Unique ecosystems such as coral reefs are part of the ocean's biodiversity wealth.
Oceans support biodiversity and sustain numerous plant and animal species along with human needs.
Offshore oil and gas serve today, while tides and waves hold immense potential for renewable blue energy.
slides.note: Reefs are like underwater treasure vaults, handle with care.

slides.title: What Is the Blue Economy
bullets: The World Bank defines Blue Economy as the sustainable use of ocean resources to promote economic growth, improved livelihoods and jobs.
It insists on preserving the health of the marine ecosystem while economies grow.
Blue Economy links three goals at once: economic growth, ecosystem health, and improved livelihoods and jobs.
slides.note: Kamana bhi, surakshit bhi, that is the Blue Economy way.

slides.title: SDG 14: Life Below Water
slides.kicker: A global promise for the seas
bullets: The Blue Economy concept is enshrined in the UN Sustainable Development Goal 14, called Life Below Water.
SDG 14 aims to reduce marine pollution and address ocean acidification.
It also asks countries to regulate fishing and protect marine ecosystems.
slides.note: SDG 14 is the ocean's very own goal.

slides.title: Aims of SDG 14
bullets: Key aims of SDG 14 include protecting marine ecosystems and conserving marine areas.
Countries are urged to eliminate harmful subsidies that damage ocean life.
The goal also wants countries to increase economic benefits from sustainable use of marine resources.
slides.note: Harmful subsidies badalte hi ocean ki saans aaram se aati hai.

slides.title: The Nautical Mile
slides.kicker: Sea distances need a sea ruler
bullets: A nautical mile is a unit of measurement used in maritime and air navigation.
It is defined as exactly 1,852 metres, which is about 6,076 feet.
Based on the Earth's circumference, one nautical mile corresponds to one minute of latitude.
This makes it a convenient unit for charting and navigation across the world's seas.
slides.note: Flight tracking apps bhi nautical miles hi dikhate hain!

slides.title: Zones Drawn by Law
slides.kicker: Who owns the ocean, and where?
bullets: Maritime zones are different areas of the ocean defined by international law.
Moving out from the coast, the zones are internal waters, territorial sea, contiguous zone, EEZ and then the high seas.
Distances of each zone are measured in nautical miles from a country's baseline.
slides.note: Farther from shore, less national control.

slides.title: Territorial and Contiguous Waters
slides.kicker: The first 24 miles are watched closely
bullets: Territorial waters extend up to 12 nautical miles, where the country has near-complete control.
Here the government can make laws relating to customs, immigration and pollution control.
The contiguous zone extends from the baseline up to 24 nautical miles.
In the contiguous zone the country has limited control over customs, fiscal matters and illegal immigration.

slides.title: The Right of Innocent Passage
bullets: Innocent passage lets foreign ships pass through territorial waters as long as they do not threaten peace, good order or security.
Ships must move continuously without stopping, except in emergencies or cases of breakdowns.
This right does not permit fishing, military operations or other non-peaceful actions.

slides.title: The Exclusive Economic Zone
bullets: EEZs extend from the baseline up to 200 nautical miles from the coast.
They are defined under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, UNCLOS, by global agreement.
The coastal country has special rights to use ocean resources such as fish, oil and gas.
Ships of other countries may still pass through peacefully, but the country does not fully own or control the EEZ waters.

slides.title: High Seas: Global Commons
bullets: Beyond the EEZs of all countries lie the high seas, also called international waters, covering about 64 per cent of the world's oceans.
These waters do not belong to any single country and are considered part of the global commons.
All countries enjoy equal rights there: navigation, fishing, flying over, laying undersea cables, and exploring for minerals.
Countries may also build lawful structures such as artificial lands, though overfishing and illegal fishing remain challenges.
slides.note: Sabka saagar, to sabka dhyan bhi.

slides.title: Law That Rules the Waves
bullets: Countries follow a set of international rules and agreements known as maritime law or maritime regulations.
These laws regulate how ships operate and move, and protect the marine environment.
They address piracy, terrorism, natural disasters and accidents, and safeguard trade routes.
Maritime disputes are conflicts between countries over territory, resources or rights in oceans, seas or coastal regions.

slides.title: COLREGs: Rules of the Road
bullets: COLREGs, the Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, are the rules of the road at sea.
They require a proper lookout, a safe speed, and deciding which side to pass on.
Ships identify the give-way and stand-on vessels so both know who should act to avoid a collision.
Lights, sound signals, shapes and radio communication help share information in crowded or hazardous waters.

items: Use lights, sound signals and radio

slides.title: MARPOL Keeps Seas Clean
bullets: Ships must meet safety standards and are prohibited from polluting the seas.
MARPOL is the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships.
It is an important international agreement aimed at reducing pollution from ships.
Together with COLREGs, it keeps both the voyage and the water safe.
slides.note: Safar bhi surakshit, samudra bhi swachh.

slides.title: Why Maritime Rules Matter
bullets: International maritime rules keep the oceans safe and ensure the fair and sustainable use of ocean resources.
They enable countries to cooperate on marine resources while protecting marine life, ships, sailors and coastal communities.
Without such regulations, oceans could become dangerous and chaotic, with increased pollution, accidents, collisions and disputes.
By setting common standards for all ships regardless of their country, maritime rules keep oceans safe, clean and open for trade and travel.

items: Oceans open for trade and travel

slides.note: Chapter done: oceans power trade, travel, communication and climate.

examples.title: Classify the Catch
examples.problem: A fishing crew lands two species: one caught 90 m deep within the continental shelf, and one caught 320 m deep beyond the shelf. Classify both catches using the book's fish zones and name the category of marine resource they belong to.
steps: Marine resources are classified into Marine Living Resources and Marine Non-living Resources; fish belong to the living category.
Coastal or neritic fish live within the continental shelf at depths of 0 to 200 m, so the catch from 90 m is a coastal or neritic fish.
Oceanic fish live beyond the continental shelf at depths greater than 200 m, so the catch from 320 m is an oceanic fish.
Both are fish, so both fall under Marine Living Resources, and fish are a major source of protein for food security.
examples.answer: The 90 m catch is a coastal or neritic fish; the 320 m catch is an oceanic fish; both are Marine Living Resources.

examples.title: Convert Sea Miles to Metres
examples.problem: Using 1 nautical mile = 1,852 m, convert the outer edge of the territorial sea (12 NM), the contiguous zone (24 NM) and the EEZ (200 NM) into metres and kilometres.
steps: Territorial sea: 12 x 1,852 = 22,224 m, which is 22.224 km.
Contiguous zone: 24 x 1,852 = 44,448 m, which is 44.448 km.
Exclusive Economic Zone: 200 x 1,852 = 370,400 m, which is 370.4 km.
Each distance is measured outward from the baseline along the coast.

examples.title: Which Zone, Which Rights?
examples.problem: Scenario A: a foreign cargo ship sails straight through a country's territorial waters without stopping. Scenario B: a coast guard checks a foreign vessel 18 nautical miles from the baseline for smuggling. Identify each maritime zone and the rights that apply.
steps: Scenario A: within 12 NM is the territorial sea, where foreign ships enjoy the right of innocent passage.
The cargo ship moves continuously, stops nowhere, and does no fishing or military activity, so its passage is innocent and lawful.
Scenario B: 18 NM lies beyond 12 NM but within 24 NM, which places the vessel in the contiguous zone.
In the contiguous zone the country has limited control over customs, fiscal matters and illegal immigration, so a smuggling check is valid there.
examples.answer: Scenario A is the territorial sea where innocent passage applies; Scenario B is the contiguous zone where limited customs and immigration control applies.
